They worshiped other gods instead of him. {When they offered sacrifices,} they no longer faced the Most Holy Place where Yahweh is present in a special way. Instead, they turned their backs to that place.

They also locked the doors of the temple, and they no longer kept the lamps burning all night. They did not burn any incense to honor Yahweh, the God of us Israelites. They did not offer sacrifices to him {each morning and evening} that the priests burned completely on the altar in temple courtyard.

This made Yahweh very angry with the people who live in Jerusalem and other places in Judah. This has made the people of other nations very frightened that they will become like us. They hiss at us {in contempt}. You have experienced this personally.
That is why our enemies were able to kill our ancestors in battle. That is why they were able to capture our sons and daughters and wives and take them away to other countries.
But now I intend to make a covenant with Yahweh, the God of us Israelites, so that he will no longer be angry with us.
You who are like my sons, Yahweh has chosen you to stand in his presence as his servants. He has chosen you to serve him by offering sacrifices. So fulfill that responsibility once again right away.”

Several leaders of the Levites responded to what King Hezekiah had said. They included Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah from the descendants of Kohath. From the descendants of Merari, there were Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehallelel. From the descendants of Gershon, there were Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah.
From the descendants of Elizaphan, there were Shimri and Jeiel. From the descendants of Asaph, there were Zechariah and Mattaniah.
From the descendants of Heman, there were Jehiel and Shimei. From the descendants of Jeduthun, there were Shemaiah and Uzziel.

Those men gathered their fellow Levites, and they all washed themselves to become ritually clean. Then they went to the temple area to remove everything that people had been using to worship idols. They worked to restore the arrangements for worship that Yahweh had described in the law of Moses. That is what the king had commanded them to do.

The priests went into the temple building to make it a holy place again. They brought out to the temple courtyard everything that they found inside the temple that people had been using to worship idols. Then the Levites took those things out of the city down to the Kidron Valley {and burned them there}.

The priests and Levites began this work on the first day of the first month of the year. It took them eight days to clear out the temple courtyard. It took them another eight days to clear out the temple building. But by the sixteenth day of that month, they had finished making Yahweh’s temple once again a special place for him.

Representatives of the priests and Levites went to the royal palace to speak with King Hezekiah.. They told him, “We have now removed everything idolatrous from everywhere in the temple area. This includes the altar on which the priests completely burn sacrifices and all the tools that the priests use to do that. It also includes the table on which the priests display fresh bread before Yahweh each week and all the tools that the priests use to do that.

When Ahaz was our king, he disobeyed God, and he discarded all the items that the priests used in the temple area. But we have {found and} repaired those items, and we have dedicated them for the priests to use again. We have put them back in front of Yahweh’s altar.”
Early the next morning, King Hezekiah gathered the city officials together. They all went to the courtyard of the temple.

They brought with them seven bulls, seven rams, and seven male lambs. They also brought seven male goats. Those goats would be an offering to ask Yahweh to forgive the sins that the king and the people of Judah had committed. This offering was also to ask Yahweh to accept the temple once again as a place where people would worship him. The king commanded the {legitimate} priests, who were descendants of Aaron, to offer those animals as sacrifices to Yahweh on the altar.

So first the city officials slaughtered the bulls, and the priests took the blood from them and sprinkled it on the altar. Then the officials slaughtered the rams, and the priests sprinkled their blood on the altar. Then the officials slaughtered the lambs, and the priests sprinkled their blood on the altar.

The goats were to be an offering to ask Yahweh to forgive the sins of the Judeans. Someone led the goats in front of the king and the people who had gathered in the temple courtyard. The king and the people laid their hands on those goats.

Then the priests slaughtered the goats and sprinkled their blood on the altar. They did that as an offering to ask Yahweh to forgive the sins that all the Israelites had committed. They did that because the king had told them to burn the animals completely on the altar and make this sin offering on behalf of all the people of Israel.

The king had told the Levites to stand in the temple courtyard with cymbals, lyres, and harps. That was what King David and his prophets Gad and Nathan had commanded. They gave this commandment by Yahweh’s authority, in obedience to the messages that he had given to his prophets.
So some Levites were standing in the temple courtyard with the musical instruments that King David had provided. The priests had trumpets.

Then Hezekiah told the priests to burn the animals completely on the altar. As soon as they started to do that, those Levites began to play the instruments that David had provided when he was the king of Israel. Some other Levites started to sing to praise Yahweh, and the priests played their trumpets, following the tune that those Levites were playing on their instruments.

While the Levites sang and the priests played their trumpets, people throughout the crowd kept bowing down to worship Yahweh. They continued to do that until the priests had finished burning all the animals completely on the altar.
When they finished burning all the animals, the king and all the city officials knelt down and worshiped Yahweh.

Then King Hezekiah and the city officials told the Levites to praise Yahweh by singing songs that David and the prophet Asaph had composed. So the Levites sang those songs, and they and the people became joyful, and the people bowed down and worshiped Yahweh.

Then Hezekiah said to everyone who was present, “You have now dedicated yourselves to worship only Yahweh. So bring forward to the temple courtyard animals to provide meat for feasts to thank Yahweh for what he has done for you.” So the people brought forward animals to sacrifice for meals to thank Yahweh. Some who wished also brought animals for the priests to burn completely on the altar.
Altogether the people brought 70 bulls, 100 rams, and 200 male lambs for the priests to burn completely on the altar as sacrifices to Yahweh.
The people brought 600 bulls and 3,000 sheep to provide meat for feasts to thank Yahweh.

It was the duty of the priests to remove the skins from the animals that they burned completely on the altar. However, the Levites had been more eager to make themselves ritually clean than the priests had been. As a result, there were not enough priests available to skin all the animals that the people offered. So the Levites, their kinsmen, helped them complete this work. They continued to help them until enough priests had made themselves ritually clean.

The Levites also helped the priests skin the animals because there were so many of them to burn completely on the altar. The priests also had to prepare offerings of wine to accompany the sacrifice of each of those animals. They also had to burn on the altar the fat from the animals that provided the meat for the feasts.
Because they had been able to restore the worship at the temple so quickly, Hezekiah and the people of Judah recognized that God had enabled them to do this, and this made them very happy.

King Hezekiah wanted people throughout the kingdoms of Israel and Judah to come and celebrate the Passover festival at the temple in Jerusalem to honor Yahweh their God. He would send messengers to invite them, and he would write a special letter to the people of the northern kingdom of Israel. However, not enough of the priests had yet made themselves ritually clean, and it would take time for people to travel to Jerusalem. So they could not celebrate the festival during the first month of the year {as the law specified}. Instead, the king and his officials and the people of Jerusalem decided to celebrate Passover the following month.
The king and the people agreed that this was a good plan.

So they resolved to send messengers throughout the land of Israel, from Beersheba {in the far south} to Dan {in the far north}. Those messengers invited people to come to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover to honor Yahweh their God. They sent the messengers because previously people from throughout Israel had not come to celebrate Passover, even though Moses wrote in the law that they should.

Obeying the king’s command, messengers went throughout Israel and Judah. They brought letters that the king and his officials had written. The letters said, “Yahweh is the God whom {your ancestors} Abraham, Isaac, and Israel worshiped. The kings of Assyria have taken away many of your people, but the rest of you are still living in your land. If you Israelites become loyal to Yahweh again, he will protect you.

Do not be like your ancestors and your kinsmen, who worshiped gods other than Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped. You know that as a result, Yahweh punished them so severely that other people are now afraid of becoming like them.

So do not be stubborn as your ancestors were. Pledge your loyalty to Yahweh again. Come to his temple, which he has set apart for his honor forever, to worship Yahweh your God. If you do that, he will no longer be angry with you.

Indeed, if you are loyal to Yahweh again, the enemies who took away your kinsmen and your children will act kindly toward them. They will allow them to return to this land. This will happen because Yahweh your God is kind and merciful. If you become loyal to him again, he will treat you favorably.”

The messengers went to cities throughout the northern kingdom of Israel as far north as the territory of the tribe of Zebulun. However, most of the people they spoke to laughed at them and ridiculed them.
However, some people from the tribes of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun were sorry for their sins, and they came to Jerusalem.
And God influenced the people of Judah to make them willing together to obey the command of the king and his officials and do what Yahweh’s law required.
As a result, many people gathered in Jerusalem in the second month of the year to celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread. They were a very large crowd of people.

First, they removed the altars that were in Jerusalem {for offering sacrifices} to false gods. They also removed all the altars for burning incense to false gods. They burned those altars in the Kidron Valley.

Then they killed the Passover lambs, on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and Levites who had not yet washed themselves to become ritually clean felt shame. They did wash themselves, and they brought animals to the temple {as sacrifices for their sins} that the priests burned completely on the altar.

Moses, that special servant of God, had written in the law where the priests should stand. The priests stood in those places. The Levites handed them bowls containing the blood {from lambs they had killed}, and the priests sprinkled that blood on the altar.

The Levites had killed those lambs because many people in the crowd had not become ritually clean, so they could not kill the lambs themselves as sacrifices to Yahweh {as the law directed}. As a result, the Levites were responsible for killing the Passover lambs for them.

In fact, many of the people had not become ritually clean. Many of them had come from the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun. But they ate the Passover meal anyway, even though Moses had written in the law that people had to be clean to eat it. But Hezekiah prayed for those people. He prayed, “Yahweh, you always do what is right. I ask you to forgive
everyone who sincerely wants to honor you, Yahweh, the God whom his ancestors worshiped. Please do that even if they have not purified themselves as they should in order to worship at your temple.”
Yahweh agreed to do what Hezekiah asked, and he did not punish the people.

The Israelites who had come to Jerusalem celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread very happily for seven days. The priests and Levites sang to praise Yahweh each day and played loud musical instruments that belonged to Yahweh’s temple.

Hezekiah thanked all those Levites for devoting themselves to Yahweh and leading the people in worship so skillfully. For those seven days, the people celebrated the Passover festival. They sacrificed fellowship offerings and thanked Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped.
Then the people who had gathered in Jerusalem agreed to celebrate for seven more days. So they celebrated joyfully for seven more days.

So that they could do that, King Hezekiah provided 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep for the people to eat during the festival. The leaders also provided 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep for the people to eat. Many priests made themselves ritually clean {so that they could serve at this festival}.

The people who had gathered from other places in Judah were very happy. So were the priests and Levites. So were the people who had come to Jerusalem from the northern kingdom of Israel. So were the foreigners who lived in that kingdom or in Judah who had come for the festival.
There had not been a celebration like this one in Jerusalem since the time when David’s son Solomon was the king of Israel. So the people at the festival were very happy.

{At the end of the festival,} the {legitimate} priests, who were descendants of Levi, stood up and asked God to make good things happen for the people. In heaven, the holy place where he lives, God heard their prayer, and he did what they asked.

After the festival ended, the Israelites who had come to Jerusalem went out to the other cities in Judah. They smashed the stone pillars that people had set up to honor false gods. They cut down the wooden images that represented the goddess Asherah. They destroyed the altars and hilltop shrines for worshiping foreign gods. They did that throughout the territory of the tribe of Judah, and also throughout the territories of Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, until none remained. Then all of those Israelites each returned to their own homes in the cities and towns where they lived.

Hezekiah organized the priests and Levites back into groups. He had each group do the work that King David had originally assigned to it. The priests would once again burn sacrifices completely on the altar and sacrifice fellowship offerings. The Levites would once again help them and also sing and play instruments to thank and praise Yahweh in the temple courtyard.

King Hezekiah contributed sheep from his own flocks for the sacrifices that the priests would burn completely on the altar. The priests offered those sacrifices in the morning and in the evening each day. They also offered them on Sabbath days, on New Moon festivals, and at each of the feasts that the Israelites celebrated each year. Moses had written in Yahweh’s law that they should do that.

Hezekiah commanded the people who lived in Jerusalem to bring the priests and Levites the part of their crops that belonged to them. That would allow them to do the work that Yahweh’s law had assigned to them.

As soon as the Israelites heard this command, they generously contributed the first grain that they harvested and the first wine and olive oil that they produced. They also contributed honey as they acquired it. They later contributed a tenth of all the crops that had grown in their fields. When they brought this to the temple, it was a very large amount.

The people of the tribe of Judah and other Israelite tribes who were living in various cities in Judah also brought a tenth of the animals in their herds and flocks. They also contributed animals that they had set apart for Yahweh their God as freewill offerings or to pay vows. The people gave so much that they made huge piles.

They began to bring their contributions in the third month of the year{, when they celebrated the start of the harvest}. They kept contributing until the seventh month{, when they celebrated the end of the harvest}.
When Hezekiah and his officials came and saw the huge piles, they praised Yahweh and asked him to make good things happen for the people who had given these gifts.
Then Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites how they had so much food that piles of it remained.

Azariah the high priest, a descendant of Zadok, replied, “Since the time that the people started to bring their offerings to the temple, we have been able to eat all that we need and still have plenty remaining. This has happened because Yahweh has enabled his people to grow many crops. As a result, this great amount of food remains.
So Hezekiah told them to arrange to keep these supplies in storerooms at the temple. So they arranged to do that.

Then they put in those storerooms the people’s contributions of the first grain they had harvested, the tenth of their crops, and the animals that people had set apart to give to Yahweh. They did this honestly. A Levite whose name was Conaniah was in charge of these supplies. His younger brother Shimei was his assistant.

{The high priest} Azariah was in charge of everything at the temple. He and King Hezekiah appointed several men to help Conaniah and his brother Shimei manage the supplies. Those men were Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismakiah, Mahath and Benaiah.

Kore son of Imnah, a Levite who guarded the east gate of the temple courtyard, was in charge of the contributions that people made voluntarily to God. He distributed to the priests their portion of the thanksgiving offerings and the parts of sacrifices that only they could eat.

Several Levites helped him distribute the contributions to priests and Levites who were in other cities and towns. They were Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah and Shecaniah. They distributed them honestly to those groups of priests and Levites. They did not give greater amounts to more important people.

However, they did not distribute food for any males in priestly families when they came to Jerusalem to serve in the temple. Hezekiah had organized the priests back into groups based on their ancestry to perform certain duties as their daily work. Their sons who were at least three years old accompanied them.

(Hezekiah had organized the priests by ancestry based on their clans.) Those Levites also did not distribute food to Levites who were at least 20 years old who were performing the duties of their groups.

But they did distribute food to the families of the priests and Levites whom Hezekiah had organized by ancestry. This included their wives, their younger sons, and their daughters. They distributed food to the priests’ and Levites’ entire families. They did that because the priests and Levites were faithfully devoting themselves to the work at the temple.

Some {legitimate} priests who were descendants of Aaron lived in in the pasturelands around the cities of Judah. Hezekiah appointed specific men in each city to distribute food to all the men who were priests. They also distributed food to all the men who could show that they were Levites by ancestry.
Hezekiah did this kind of thing throughout Judah. He did things that Yahweh his God considered to be good, right, and honest.

Hezekiah undertook many things in order to honor God. He restored the worship at the temple, and he obeyed the commandments in the law. He did all of these things wholeheartedly. As a result, he was successful.

After King Hezekiah had done these things so loyally to Yahweh, King Sennacherib of Assyria led his army to invade Judah. He besieged the cities that had walls around them. He thought that he would capture those cities.
Hezekiah learned that Sennacherib had invaded Judah, and he recognized that he intended to attack Jerusalem.

So he discussed with his officers and soldiers what they should do. They agreed that plenty of water should not be available to the king of Assyria and his army when they got to Jerusalem. So they decided to block the springs of water that were outside the city. Many people came to help, and they blocked all the springs of water. As a result, the Gihon stream, which flowed through that area, dried up.

Then Hezekiah strengthened Jerusalem’s defenses. He had his workers repair the sections of the city wall that had damage. He also had them repair the outer wall and the defensive towers on the main walls. He had them strengthen the Millo on the east side of the City of David. He also had them make a large number of weapons and shields.

Hezekiah appointed army commanders to direct groups of people in Jerusalem {to defend the city}. He asked the people to gather in the square inside one of the city gates so that he could speak to them. He encouraged them by saying,
“Be very brave. Do not be at all afraid of the king of Assyria, even though he has a huge army with him. Recognize that Yahweh is helping us, and his power is much greater than their power.
They have only human strength, but we have Yahweh our God helping us and fighting battles for us.” The people became more confident because of what Hezekiah, the king of Judah, told them.

Then Sennacherib sent some of his officers to Jerusalem with a message for King Hezekiah and the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem or who had gone there for protection. Sennacherib and his army were besieging the city of Lachish at the time. But his messengers said,
“Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, says that you should not stay in Jerusalem and try to defend yourselves against his army. You should not believe that you can do that successfully.
Hezekiah is telling you that Yahweh your God will rescue you from my power. But what he says is not true. If you believe him, you will die from having no food to eat and no water to drink.

{Yahweh will not help} Hezekiah{, because he} has commanded his servants to destroy the hilltop shrines and altars where you could have worshiped Yahweh. He has told you people who live in Jerusalem and other places in Judah that you must worship and offer sacrifices only at the altar in the temple courtyard.

You must certainly know what I and the kings who ruled Assyria before me have done to the people of other countries. Certainly none of the gods that they worshiped were able to rescue them from our power. The kings who ruled before me completely destroyed many nations, and you cannot name a single god that those nations worshiped that was able to rescue them from their power. So you should not believe that your God will be able to rescue you from my power.

So do not believe what Hezekiah is telling you. If you do, he will deceive you into doing the wrong thing. Recognize that no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to rescue his people from my power or from the power of the kings who ruled Assyria before me. So your God will certainly not be able to rescue you from my power!”
Sennacherib’s officers said more bad things about Yahweh, the true God, and about Hezekiah, the king who served him loyally.

King Sennacherib also wrote letters to insult Yahweh, the God of the Israelites. He said bad things about him. He wrote, “No god of any nation anywhere else has rescued his people from my power. In the same way, the God of Hezekiah will not rescue his people from my power.”

The officers {who had come to Jerusalem} shouted in the Hebrew language to people who were standing on the city wall. They were trying to make them very afraid {so they would not fight well and} the army of Assyria would capture the city.
They talked about the God whose temple was in Jerusalem the way they talked about the gods that people worshiped in other countries. But those gods were just idols that people had made.
King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz prayed to God desperately about this.

Then Yahweh sent an angel who killed all the soldiers, officers, and commanders in the place where the army of the king of Assyria had set up its tents. This disgraced the king of Assyria, and he retreated to his own country. One day when he went into the temple of his god, some of his own sons killed him there with their swords.

That is how Yahweh rescued Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem from the power of Sennacherib, the king of Assyria. and from the power of all their other enemies. Yahweh kept the countries around them from attacking them.
After this, the people of other nations greatly respected Hezekiah. Many people brought offerings for Yahweh to Jerusalem, and they also brought valuable gifts for King Hezekiah.

Around this time, Hezekiah became so sick that he was in danger of dying. But he prayed to Yahweh, and Yahweh told him {through the prophet Isaiah} that he would live. Yahweh gave Hezekiah a special sign to confirm this.

But Hezekiah had become very proud, so he did not make an offering at the temple to thank Yahweh for helping him. This made Yahweh angry with him and with the people who lived in Jerusalem and other places in Judah.
But then Hezekiah recognized it was wrong to be so proud, and so did the people who lived in Jerusalem. So Yahweh did not punish them during the remaining years that Hezekiah was their king.
Hezekiah became very rich, and people honored him greatly. He had his workers make storerooms for his silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and other valuable things.

He also had them build buildings to store the grain, wine, and olive oil that his lands produced. He also had them make stalls for the various kinds of cattle he owned and pens for his flocks of sheep.
God enabled him to acquire so much livestock that he had his workers build enclosures where he could safely keep his large flocks of sheep and herds of cattle.

Hezekiah was the one who had his workers block the higher place where the water was flowing out of the Gihon spring and build a tunnel to bring the water {into the city} on the west side of the City of David. Hezekiah successfully completed all of his projects.

But as a result, God wanted to know what kind of person Hezekiah had become. To find out, God did not influence him to respond in a certain way when the rulers of Babylon sent messengers to him. They sent them to ask about the miracle that God had performed in the land of Judah.

The book in which the kings of Judah and Israel recorded what happened during their reigns describes further things that Hezekiah did and how he remained faithful to Yahweh. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz wrote this account of his reign.

When Hezekiah died, the Judeans buried him near the tombs where they had buried the previous kings who were descendants of David. People who lived in Jerusalem and throughout the kingdom of Judah honored him when he died. His son Manasseh became the next king.
Manasseh was 12 years old when he began to rule. He ruled Judah for 55 years in Jerusalem.
He did many things that Yahweh considered to be evil. He imitated the disgusting practices of the nations that Yahweh had forced to leave the land of Canaan so that the Israelites could settle there.

His father Hezekiah had destroyed the shrines where the Judeans had worshiped on the tops of hills. But Manasseh commanded his workers to rebuild those shrines. He had his workers build altars for Baal. He also had them set up poles for the worship of the goddess Asherah. Manasseh also bowed down to the sun, moon, and stars to worship them.

He directed his workers to build altars {for worshiping foreign gods} and to put them inside Yahweh’s temple, even though Yahweh had said, “Jerusalem will always be the place where people worship me.”
He also had his workers make altars for the sun, moon, and stars and put them in the courtyards for the priests and the people in the temple area.

He even burned his own sons as sacrifices to false gods. He did that in the Valley of Ben Hinnom. He also performed rituals and looked for omens to try to predict the future, and he practiced sorcery. He allowed people to dig pits so they could use them try to contact people who had died. People also used those pits to try to talk to spirits that they thought could tell them things that people otherwise could not know. He did very many things that Yahweh considered to be evil, and that made Yahweh very angry.

He placed inside the temple building the image he had made that represented a false god. That was the place about which God had said to David and his son Solomon, “I will make Jerusalem, and especially this temple, places where people will always worship me. I chose Jerusalem for that purpose from among all of the cities in the land of Israel.

And if the Israelite people carefully obey all my commands and all the different kinds of laws that I gave to them through Moses, I will not make them wander again. They will be able to stay in this land that I gave to their ancestors.”

But Manasseh persuaded the people who lived in Jerusalem and other places in Judah to commit sins that were even worse than the sins that the people of the nations committed whom Yahweh destroyed so that the Israelites could settle in the land of Canaan.
Yahweh sent prophets to warn Manasseh and the people of Judah, but they ignored them.

So Yahweh allowed the king of Assyria’s army commanders to lead their soldiers to attack Jerusalem. They captured Manasseh, put a hook in his nose and bronze chains on his feet, and took him to Babylon.

But there, while he was suffering, he humbled himself greatly in relationship to {Yahweh,} the God whom his ancestors had worshiped. He became loyal to Yahweh as his God and pleaded with him to help him.

When he prayed to Yahweh, Yahweh {recognized that he was sincere and} determined to help him. Yahweh did what he asked and allowed him to return to Jerusalem and rule his kingdom again. Then Manasseh realized that Yahweh is the only true God.

After Manasseh returned, he had his workers strengthen the outer wall around Jerusalem and make it much higher. The section they strengthened extended from the west side of the Gihon spring in the valley to the Fish Gate and around the {hill of} Ophel. Manasseh also appointed army commanders for all the cities in Judah that had walls around them.

Manasseh also had his workers remove from the temple the idols that represented foreign gods and the idol that he had put there. He also had them remove all the altars that he had previously told them to build on Mount Zion, where Yahweh’s temple was, and in other places in Jerusalem. He had them throw the idols and the materials from the altars out of the city.

Then he had his workers repair Yahweh’s altar {in the temple courtyard}. He offered fellowship sacrifices on it and a special sacrifice to thank Yahweh. He told the people of Judah that they must worship only Yahweh, the God of the Israelites.
Even so, the people continued to offer sacrifices at hilltop shrines, but they offered them only to Yahweh their God.

The book in which the kings of Israel recorded what happened during their reigns describes further things that Manasseh did. These things include the messages that prophets spoke to him on behalf of Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, and Manasseh’s prayer to God {for mercy when the Babylonians captured him}.

The account that the prophet Hozai made of Manasseh’s reign records the serious sins that he committed. It lists the places where he built hilltop shrines for wooden images that represented the goddess Asherah and for other idols. But this account also describes how Manasseh then humbled himself and prayed to God and how God did what he asked.
When Manasseh died, the Judeans buried him in his palace. His son Amon became the next king.
Amon was 22 years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for two years.

He did many things that Yahweh considered to be evil, as his father Manasseh had done {in the first part of his reign}. Manasseh’s workers had made many idols, and Amon sacrificed to them and worshiped them.
Amon did not humble himself in relationship to Yahweh as his father had done. Instead, he was even more sinful than his father had been.
Amon’s officials made a secret plan to kill him. They assassinated him in his palace.
But the people of Judah then executed all those who had assassinated Amon. They appointed his son Josiah to be the next king.
Josiah was 8 years old when he became the king of Judah. He ruled from Jerusalem for 31 years.
He did things that Yahweh considered to be right. He lived as his ancestor King David had lived. He did not live any differently.

After he had been ruling for almost eight years, while he was still a boy, he began to worship God sincerely, as his ancestor King David had done. Four years later, he began to make Jerusalem and the rest of the kingdom of Judah acceptable places to worship Yahweh. He did that by destroying the hilltop shrines where there were wooden images that represented the goddess Asherah, metal images, and other kinds of idols.

He personally accompanied his workers as they destroyed the altars where people worshiped Baal. There were idols representing the sun above those altars, and the workers cut them down. They smashed the wooden poles that represented the goddess Asherah, the metal images, and the other kinds of idols. They ground them into powder and spread the powder over the graves of the people who had offered sacrifices to those false gods.

They burned the bones of the priests who had offered sacrifices to those gods on the altars they had used to do that. That is how Josiah made Jerusalem and the rest of the kingdom of Judah acceptable places to worship Yahweh once again.

Then he went with his workers to the cities in the territories of the tribes of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon. They went as far north as the territory of the tribe of Naphtali. The enemies of the Israelites had attacked and ruined the cities throughout those areas.

Josiah’s workers also destroyed the altars to foreign gods in those places. They broke apart the wooden poles that represented the goddess Asherah, and they ground the idols to powder. Throughout the land of Israel, they also cut up the idols that represented the sun. Then Josiah returned to Jerusalem.

When Josiah had been ruling for almost 18 years, he decided to do something further to make his kingdom and the temple acceptable places to worship Yahweh. He sent Shaphan son of Azaliah and Maaseiah, the governor of the city, and Joah son of Joahaz, his royal secretary, to repair Yahweh’s temple.

They went to Hilkiah the high priest and gave him the money that people had brought to the temple. It was money that the Levites who guarded the entrances to the temple courtyard had collected from people who had come there. They included people from the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim and people who had survived when enemies had conquered the northern kingdom of Israel. They also included people who lived in Jerusalem and other places in the territories of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin.

Then Hilkiah and his fellow priests gave the money to the men they appointed to supervise the work of repairing the temple. Those supervisors paid the men who did the actual work of repairing and strengthening Yahweh’s temple.

They also gave some of the money to the carpenters and builders to buy stones that workers had shaped and timber for supports and beams for the temple and the buildings around it. The kings of Judah had not cared well for those buildings.

The workers did their work faithfully. The men whom the priests appointed to supervise them included the Levites Jahath and Obadiah, who were descendants of Merari. They also included Zechariah and Meshullam, who were descendants of Kohath. (People respected these Levites who were skillful at playing musical instruments.)
They also supervised the men who carried heavy loads and the foremen of all the crews that did various kinds of work. Other Levites were scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.

One day the priests went to the temple to give the supervisors money that people had brought to the temple. While he was in the temple, the high priest Hilkiah found a scroll that recorded the laws that Yahweh had given to Moses.
So Hilkiah told Shaphan, the king’s secretary, “I have found a scroll in the temple that records the laws that God gave to Moses.” Hilkiah gave the scroll to Shaphan{, and he read it}.
Then Shaphan brought the scroll to King Josiah. He started by giving him a report about the temple repairs. He told him, “I gave the priests all your instructions, and they are obeying them.

They have emptied the chest in which they were collecting money that people brought to the temple. They have given the money to the men who are supervising the work so that they can pay the workers who are repairing the temple.”
Then Shaphan also told the king, “The high priest Hilkiah gave me this scroll.” And Shaphan read to the king what the scroll recorded.
When the king heard the laws that Shaphan was reading to him from the scroll, he tore his robes {to show how concerned he was that Yahweh would punish the Judeans}.
Then King Josiah gave special instructions to Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Akbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan his royal secretary, and Asaiah, his special advisor. He told them,

“Now that Hilkiah has found this scroll, I want you to go and ask Yahweh what I and the surviving Israelites and the people of Judah should do about what it says. Our ancestors did not obey Yahweh’s commandments. They should have done everything that this scroll records. So Yahweh must be very angry with us.”

So Hilkiah and the other men whom the king had sent went to consult a woman whose name was Huldah. She was a prophetess, and she lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem. She was the wife of Shallum, whose father was Tikvah and whose grandfather was Harhas. Shallum took care of the garments that the priests wore in the temple. Those five men told Huldah about the scroll that Hilkiah had found.
In response, she told them, “Yahweh, the God whom we Israelites worship, says that he wants you to say something to the man who sent you to me.

Yahweh says that he is going to make something terrible happen to this city and to the people who live here. He is going to make all the bad things happen that the scroll people read to King Josiah describes.

He is going to do that because they stopped worshiping him and burned incense to {honor} other gods. They made many idols, and that has made him very angry. He is so angry with them that he is certainly going punish them.
But there is something further that you are to tell the king of Judah, who sent you to ask Yahweh about what the scroll said. Yahweh, the God whom we Israelites worship, says that

he is going to treat him mercifully. Yahweh will do that because he was so sad and he acted humbly toward him when he heard what Yahweh said he was going to do to punish this city and the people who live here. {When King Josiah heard that,} he acted humbly toward Yahweh, and he tore his robes {to show his distress}, and he wept. He knew that Yahweh was watching him. That is why Yahweh declares {that he is going to treat him mercifully}.

Yahweh wants you to tell Josiah that he is going to allow him to die {before this happens}, and the Judeans will bury him peacefully. Yahweh is still going to cause many terrible things to happen to Jerusalem and the people who live in it. But Josiah will not be alive to see that.” The officials returned to King Josiah and reported what Huldah had told them.
Then King Josiah sent messengers to summon all the elders of Jerusalem and the other places in the kingdom of Judah.

The king went to the temple courtyard. A great crowd of many different kinds of people from Jerusalem and other places in Judah assembled there with him. Many priests and Levites were there along with ordinary people. While they all listened, the king read to them all the laws that the scroll recorded that Yahweh had given the Israelites when he made his solemn agreement with them. Hilkiah had found that scroll in the temple.

The king was standing next to a pillar {on the temple porch}. He made a solemn agreement with Yahweh that he would live as Yahweh wanted him to live. He promised to obey all of Yahweh’s laws wholeheartedly and enthusiastically. In that way, the terms of the solemn agreement that the scroll from the temple described became the law of Israel once again.

King Josiah made the people who had gathered from Judah and Benjamin to the temple courtyard promise to obey that solemn agreement. From then on, the people who lived in Jerusalem {and in the rest of the kingdom} obeyed the solemn agreement that they had made with Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped.

Josiah ordered his workers to remove all the disgusting idols from throughout the territory of the Israelites. He commanded everyone who lived in his kingdom to worship only Yahweh as their God. For as long as Josiah was alive, the people did not worship gods other than Yahweh, the God whom their ancestors had worshiped.

Then Josiah arranged for the people to celebrate the Passover Festival in Jerusalem to honor Yahweh. They slaughtered the lambs for the Passover feast on the fourteenth day of the first month {of the year}.
Josiah told the priests to resume the work that they each did at the temple. He encouraged them to do their work well.

The Levites had special work to do for Yahweh, including teaching the Israelites. But they had been carrying the sacred chest around {on poles} on their shoulders {to keep it safe}. But Josiah told them, “You may now put the sacred chest {safely} back in the temple that Solomon son of David built when he was the king of Israel. You may now devote yourselves to serving Yahweh your God and his Israelite people.
Get ready {to help the people celebrate Passover}. When David and his son Solomon were kings of Israel, they wrote instructions for the work that each of your clans should do.

I want each of your clans to stand {in a different part of} the temple area. I am going to have your fellow Israelites who are not priests or Levites gather in the temple area according to their own clans. Part of each of your clans should help one of those family groups.

To provide a Passover feast for your fellow Israelites, kill the animals for the meal. Then wash yourselves {and hand their blood to the priests}. Do what Yahweh told Moses that the Israelites should do.”

Josiah provided 30,000 young sheep and goats from his own flocks. These were enough for the Passover meals for all the Israelites who came for the feast. He also provided 3,000 bulls from his own herds {as fellowship sacrifices}.

His officials also voluntarily contributed animals for the people, the priests, and the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel were important officials at the temple. They gave 2,600 young sheep and goats to provide Passover meals for the priests. They also gave 300 bulls {for fellowship sacrifices}.

Some of the leaders of the Levites gave 5,000 sheep and goats to provide Passover meals for the Levites. These men were Conaniah, his younger brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad. They also gave 300 bulls {for fellowship sacrifices}.

This is how they arranged for the Passover meal. The priests stood in their places. The Levites gathered in their clans {in order to help various family groups}. That is what the king had commanded them to do.
The Levites killed the Passover lambs and goats and handed their blood {in bowls} to the priests, who sprinkled the blood on the altar. The Levites removed the skins from the animals,

and they also removed the parts of the animals that the priests would burn completely on the altar. They gave those parts to the various family groups that they were assisting. The families then offered those parts to Yahweh in order to obey the instructions that Moses had written in the law. The priests, Levites, and people did the same thing with the oxen.

As the law required, the Levites roasted the meat from the lambs and goats for the Passover meal over an open fire. But they cooked differently the meat from the animals that the king and officials had consecrated for fellowship offerings. They boiled that meat in pots and kettles and pans. The Levites served both kinds of meat immediately to all the people who had come for the feast.

The priests, the descendants of Aaron, were busy for the entire day burning the parts of the animals that belonged to Yahweh, including their fat, completely on the altar. {Since they did not have the opportunity to prepare their own meals,} after the Levites had prepared meals for the people, they prepared meals for themselves and for the priests.

The singers who were descendants of Asaph stayed in the places where King David, Asaph, Heman, and the king’s prophet Jeduthun had commanded them to stand {and sing}. The Levites who guarded each of the gates of the temple courtyard remained at their positions. Their fellow Levites prepared food for them to eat, so the singers and gatekeepers did not need to leave their places.

On that day, the priests, Levites, and people did everything necessary to celebrate the Passover Festival to honor Yahweh. That is what King Josiah had commanded them to do. They also presented offerings that the priests burned completely on Yahweh’s altar.
The Israelites who came for the feast celebrated the Passover on that day, and then they celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

The Israelites had not celebrated a Passover Festival like this one since the time when the prophet Samuel lived. None of the kings of Israel had celebrated the Passover as Josiah did with the priests, the Levites, and the other people of Judah and Israel who came to Jerusalem to celebrate with the people who lived there.
They celebrated this Passover Festival when Josiah had been ruling for almost 18 years.

Josiah did all these things to restore the worship of Yahweh at his temple. Some time later, King Neco of Egypt led his soldiers to fight {the Babylonians} at the city of Carchemish near the Euphrates River. Josiah led his army to fight against them.

Neco sent some messengers to tell Josiah, “I have no quarrel with you, King of Judah. I have not come now to attack you. Instead, I am going to fight against my enemy, the king of Babylon. God has told me to hurry. So stop opposing God, who is helping me. Otherwise, God will kill you.”

But Josiah did not do what Neco told him to do, even though God was speaking through him. He did not return to Jerusalem with his army. But he disguised himself in order to fight against Neco. He led his soldiers to fight against Neco’s army at the plain of Megiddo.
As the Egyptian archers were shooting at the Judean soldiers, one of them hit King Josiah. He told his officers, “I am badly wounded, so take me away from here.”

So they took him out of his war chariot and put him in his traveling chariot. They brought him to Jerusalem, where he died. The Judeans buried him in the royal tombs. People throughout Jerusalem and other places in Judah mourned for him.

The prophet Jeremiah composed a sad song about Josiah because he had died. Many men and women still sing sad songs that tell about Josiah. The Judean leaders gave orders to teach these songs to the people. The collection of laments records them.

The book in which the kings of Israel and Judah recorded what happened during their reigns describes further things that Josiah did throughout his reign. This includes how he faithfully obeyed Yahweh’s laws, which Moses wrote down.
Then the Judeans appointed Josiah’s son Jehoahaz as the next king in Jerusalem.
Joahaz was 23 years old when he became the king, but he ruled in Jerusalem for only three months.
Then the king of Egypt came and took him away. He also forced the people of Judah to pay him three and one third metric tons of silver and thirty-three kilograms of gold.

The king of Egypt appointed Jehoahaz’s younger brother Eliakim to be the next king of the people who lived in Jerusalem and in other places in Judah. He changed Eliakim’s name to Jehoiakim. But Neco took Joahaz to Egypt as his prisoner.
Jehoiakim was 25 years old when he became the king of Judah, and he ruled from Jerusalem for 11 years. He did many things that Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, considered to be evil.
Then the army of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon attacked Jehoiakim’s army. They captured Jehoiakim, bound him with bronze chains, and took him away to Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar’s soldiers also took some of the articles that the priests used in Yahweh’s temple. They brought them to Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar put them in the temple of his god.

The book in which the kings of Israel and Judah recorded what happened during their reigns describes further things that Jehoiakim did. This includes the disgusting acts he committed and what a bad person he was. His son Jehoiachin became the next king of Judah.
Jehoiachin was 18 years old when he became the king of Judah. He ruled from Jerusalem for only three months and ten days. He did many things that Yahweh considered to be evil.

During the spring of the next year, King Nebuchadnezzar sent soldiers to bring him to Babylon. They also took away many valuable things from Yahweh’s temple. Nebuchadnezzar appointed Jehoiachin’s uncle Zedekiah to rule instead over the people who lived in Jerusalem and in other parts of Judah.
Zedekiah was 21 years old when he became the king, and he ruled from Jerusalem for 11 years.

He did many things that Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, considered to be evil. Yahweh gave the prophet Jeremiah a message to warn him. But when Zedekiah heard that message, he was not sorry for the wrong things he had been doing.

He was very proud, and he was very stubborn. So he did not start obeying Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, once again. King Nebuchadnezzar had made him promise to be loyal to him. He had made him say that he hoped God would punish him if he broke that promise. Even so, Zedekiah rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar.

Most of the leaders of the priests and the people of Judah also did many very wicked things. They did the same kind of disgusting things as the people had done whom Yahweh forced to leave the land of Canaan. Yahweh had made his temple in Jerusalem a special place where he was present. But those leaders put idols in the temple area, so that Yahweh no longer considered it an acceptable place to worship him.

Yahweh was the God whom the ancestors of the people of Judah had worshiped. He wanted to be merciful to his people, and he did not want anyone to destroy his temple. So he continually sent prophets to them with messages to warn them.

But the people laughed at the prophets. They treated God’s messages as if they were not important. They treated the prophets very badly. Finally Yahweh became so angry with his people that he decided he would certainly destroy Judah.

He influenced the king of Babylon to attack Judah with his army. They killed the Judean soldiers with their swords, even those who went to the temple area for safety. They did not spare anyone, regardless of their sex or age. God enabled the army of Nebuchadnezzar to conquer the entire city.

His soldiers took to Babylon all the items of every size that the priests used in God’s temple. They also took the valuable things that were in the storerooms at the temple and the valuable things that belonged to the king and his officials.
They burned the temple, and they broke down the wall around Jerusalem. They burned all the important buildings in Jerusalem, and they destroyed all the valuable things that they did not carry away.

There were some people whom the soldiers had not killed. They took those people away as prisoners to Babylon. Those people had to work for Nebuchadnezzar and the kings who ruled Babylon after him until the army of Persia conquered Babylon.

Those people remained in Babylon for 70 years. During that time, no one planted or harvested crops in their land. As a result, the soil recovered, as if would have done if the people had obeyed the law of Moses and not planted crops every seventh year. Yahweh had said through Jeremiah that this would happen, and it did.

During the first year after Cyrus, king of Persia, {conquered the kingdom of Babylon,} Yahweh motivated Cyrus to write a message. Yahweh did this in order to make something happen that Jeremiah had predicted. Cyrus sent messengers throughout his empire with copies of the message, and he ordered them to proclaim it as they went. This is what they proclaimed:

“I, King Cyrus, rule the Persian Empire, and I say, ‘Yahweh, the God who is in heaven, has made me ruler over the great kingdoms of this part of the world. Now he has assigned me to {make sure that his people} build a temple for him in {the city of} Jerusalem in {the province of} Judah. Any of you who belong to his people may go {to Jerusalem in Judah to rebuild this temple for Yahweh}. And may Yahweh your God help you!’”

During the first year after Cyrus, king of Persia, {conquered the kingdom of Babylon,} Yahweh motivated Cyrus to write a message. Yahweh did this in order to fulfill a prophecy that Jeremiah had spoken. Cyrus sent messengers throughout his empire with copies of the message and he ordered them to proclaim it as they went. This is what they proclaimed:

“I, King Cyrus, rule the Persian Empire, and I say this: Yahweh, the God who is in heaven, has made me ruler over the great kingdoms of this part of the world. Now he has assigned me to {make sure that his people} build a temple for him in {the city of} Jerusalem in {the province of} Judah.

All you people who belong to God may go up to Jerusalem in Judah to rebuild this temple for Yahweh. He is the God who is in Jerusalem, the God whom the people of Israel worship. And may God give you success!

There are other people who are living around the Israelites in the places where the Israelites have been living since their ancestors were exiled here. Those people must contribute silver and gold to the Israelites who go. They must also give to the Israelites animals and {any} supplies {that they might need}. They should also give them other gifts that they can use to help build the temple of God in Jerusalem.”

Then God motivated some of the priests and Levites and {some of} the clan leaders from {the tribes of} Judah and Benjamin to return to Jerusalem. Those whom God motivated got ready to return to Jerusalem and build the temple for him there.

Many of their neighbors helped them by giving them silver and golden things, animals, and supplies for the journey. They also gave them other valuable gifts, and they gave them money to buy things for building the temple.

King Cyrus also commanded {his servants} to bring out the valuable things that King Nebuchadnezzar{’s soldiers} had taken from the temple of Yahweh in Jerusalem and had put in the temples of their gods {in Babylon}.

{Specifically,} King Cyrus of Persia commanded Mithredath, his treasurer, {to command his servants} to bring out all of these items and to give each one of them to Sheshbazzar, the leader of {the group that was going to return to} Judah.
This is a list of the items {that Cyrus donated}: 30 gold basins, 1,000 silver basins, 29 knives,
30 gold bowls, 410 secondary silver bowls, and 1,000 other utensils.
All together, Cyrus gave 5, 400 silver and gold items to Sheshbazzar to take with him when he and the others returned from {the kingdom of} Babylon to Jerusalem.

{Many years ago, the army of} King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had captured many Israelite people and taken them away to the kingdom of Babylon. Now, these Israelite people began to return to Judah. Some returned to Jerusalem, and some returned to other places in Judah. Each of them went to the towns where their ancestors had lived. This is a list of the groups who returned.
The leaders of those people who returned were Zerubbabel, Joshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah.
2, 812 descendants of Pahath-Moab, from the families of Jeshua and Joab,
98 descendants of Ater, who descended from Hezekiah,
{The following is a list of people whose ancestors had lived in these towns in Judah:}
743 from Kiriath Arim, Kephirah, and Beeroth,
These are the priests who returned:
These are the descendants of Levi who returned:
128 musicians who were descendants of Asaph,
139 gatekeepers who were descendants of the gatekeepers Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai,
The following is a list of the temple workers who returned. They were the descendants of these men: Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth,
The following descendants of King Solomon’s servants returned {to Jerusalem}. They were the descendants of these men: Sotai, Hassophereth, Peruda,
Shephatiah, Hattil, Pochereth Hazzebaim, and Ami.
Altogether, there were 392 descendants of temple workers and Solomon’s servants who returned.
There was another group that returned {to Judah} from {the towns of} Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cerub, Addon, and Immer {in Babylonia}. But they could not prove that they were genuine Israelites.
This group included 652 people who were descendants of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda.

The descendants of the priests in this group included people belonging to Habaiah’s clan, Hakkoz’s clan, and Barzillai’s clan. Barzillai had married a woman who was a descendant of Barzillai from the region of Gilead. He had taken the name of his father-in-law’s clan for himself.

The people in this group searched in the documents that listed the names {of the descendants} from the {various Israelite} clans, but they did not find {their names there}. So the officials did not permit them to do the work that priests did.

The governor told these men that they could not eat the shares of the sacrifices that only the priests could eat until a {high} priest could consult Yahweh by using the sacred lots {to determine that they truly were descendants of priestly families. Only if the high priest determined that these men truly were priests could they eat the most sacred food}.
Altogether in this group, 42, 360 Israelite people returned to Judah.
The Israelites also brought along with them 7, 337 male and female servants and 200 male and female musicians.
The Israelites also brought with them {from Babylonia} 736 horses, 245 mules,

When they arrived at {the ruins of} the temple of Yahweh in Jerusalem, some of the clan leaders gave money for the supplies needed to rebuild the temple in the same place where the old temple had been.
Each one gave as much as he was able to give for the work {on the temple}. Altogether, they gave 61,000 gold coins, 5,000 silver bars, and 100 robes for the priests.

So all of these priests, Levites, musicians, gatekeepers, temple servants, and other people returned to live in the towns and villages {of the province of Judah}. They settled in the places where their ancestors had lived.
After the Israelite people {returned and} began to live in their towns, in the autumn of that year, they all gathered together in Jerusalem.

Then Joshua son of Jehozadak and his fellow priests and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his associates all began to rebuild the altar of the God of Israel. They did that so that they could sacrifice burnt offerings on it. They wanted to follow what the prophet Moses had written in the laws that God had given to him.

Even though they were afraid of the people who were already living in that area, they rebuilt the altar at the same place where the previous altar had been. They began to offer sacrifices to Yahweh on it every morning and every evening.

{Fifteen days after they started to offer these sacrifices,} the people celebrated the Festival of Shelters. {Moses had commanded them to do this in the decrees that God had given to him.} Each day the priests offered the sacrifices that were required for that day.

From then on, they presented the regular burnt offerings and the {other required} offerings{. These were} for the New Moon festivals and the other festivals that they celebrated as special times each year to honor Yahweh. They also brought other offerings to Yahweh just because they wanted to{, not because they were required to bring them}.
But even though they started bringing burnt offerings to Yahweh at the beginning of autumn, they had not yet started rebuilding the temple.

So the {leaders of the} Israelites hired stone-cutters and carpenters {to do the construction work}. They also bought logs of cedar trees from the people of {the cities of} Tyre and Sidon. To pay for the logs, the Israelites sent grain, wine, and olive oil to those people. Since King Cyrus had said that the Israelites could buy these things, the people of Tyre and Sidon {agreed. They} brought the logs down from the mountains in Lebanon to the seashore at Joppa and then floated them along the coast to {the city of} Joppa. {Then they brought the logs inland from Joppa up to Jerusalem.}

The Israelites started to rebuild the temple in the second month of the second year after they had returned to Jerusalem. Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, Joshua the son of Jozadak, their fellow leaders the priests and the Levites, and all the people who had come from where their enemies had taken them to Jerusalem supported this project. The leaders assigned the Levites who were twenty years old and older to supervise this work of rebuilding the temple for Yahweh.

Jeshua, his sons, and his other relatives, and Kadmiel and his sons together helped to supervise those who were doing the work on the temple. They were all descendants of Judah. The sons and grandsons of Henadad along with the rest of their fellow Levites {joined in the work}.

When the builders finished laying the foundation of the temple of Yahweh, the priests and the Levites did what King David had told Asaph and the other musicians to do {many years previously} in order to praise Yahweh. The priests put on their robes and stood in their places, blowing their trumpets. Then the Levites who were descendants of Asaph clashed their cymbals.

Then the Levites praised Yahweh and thanked him by singing this song about him: “He is very good to us! He will continue to be faithful and kind to us Israelites {and he will love us} forever.” Then all the people shouted loudly. They praised Yahweh because they had finished laying the foundation of his temple.

Many of the old priests, Levites, and leaders of families remembered seeing the first temple. They cried aloud when they saw the workers lay the foundation of this temple {because they thought that this temple would not be as big or as beautiful as the first temple}. But the other people shouted joyfully in loud voices.

Since the shouting was so loud, no one could tell the difference between the people who were shouting joyfully and the people who were crying sorrowfully. All the noise was so loud that even people far away could hear it.

The enemies of {the people of the tribes of} Judah and Benjamin learned that the Israelites who had returned from Babylon were rebuilding the temple for Yahweh, the God whom the people of Israel worship.

So they approached Zerubbabel the governor and the other clan leaders and {deceptively} said to them, “We want to help you to build the temple. After all, we also worship your God. We have been offering sacrifices to him since the time that Esarhaddon, the king of Assyria, brought us here.”

But Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the other Jewish clan leaders replied, “We will not allow you to help us build a temple for our God. No, we alone will build it for Yahweh, the God whom Israel worships, because that is what King Cyrus of Persia told us to do.”
Then the people who had been living in that land {before the Israelites returned there} started doing things to make the Jews discouraged and afraid to continue building {the temple}.

They bribed government officials to prevent the Jews from fulfilling their plans {to rebuild the temple and the city}. They did that all during the time that Cyrus was king of Persia, and continued to do it during {the time of the kings after him, including} the time when Darius was king of Persia.

These enemies of the Jews continued to accuse them during the time that {Darius’ son} Ahasuerus was king. When Ahasuerus became king, they wrote a letter to him in which they accused the people living in the province of Judah and the city of Jerusalem {of planning to rebel against the government}.

Then again during the time of Artaxerxes, {who was the next} king of Persia, the enemies of the Jews wrote a letter to him. Some men named Bishlam, Mithredath, and Tabeel were the leaders of this group. They had someone write the letter for them in the Aramaic language, using the Aramaic alphabet.

Rehum, the high commissioner, and Shimshai, the provincial secretary, agreed that they could write the letter to King Artaxerxes {with their authority} to protest about what was happening in Jerusalem. This is what they wrote:

From Rehum the high commissioner, Shimshai the provincial secretary, and others with us who are judges and other government officials{. We represent the people} from {the areas of} Persia, Erech, Babylon, and Susa in the district of Elam,

as well as the other people groups whom the great and glorious Ashurbanipal had deported and sent to live in cities in Samaria and in the rest of the province west of the {Euphrates} River. Therefore:
(This is what they wrote in the letter that they sent to him:)

“Your Majesty, we want you to know that the Jews who left from your territories are now living near us. They are rebuilding the city of Jerusalem. These people are wicked and want to rebel against you. Therefore, they are now rebuilding the walls {of that city} and repairing the foundations {of its buildings}.
It is important for you to know that if they rebuild this city and finish building its walls, they will stop paying any taxes. As a result, there will be less money in your treasury.
So, because we are loyal to you, and because we do not want anyone to humiliate you, for these reasons we are sending this information to you.

We suggest that you {order your officials to} search among the records that your predecessors kept. {If you do that,} you will find out that the people in this city have always rebelled against their rulers. You will find out that these people have withheld taxes from kings and from rulers of provinces. You will find out that from long ago the leaders of this city have started rebellions. That is the reason why {the Babylonian army} destroyed this city.
We want you to know that if they rebuild this city and finish building its walls, then you will no longer be able to control {any of the people in} this province west of the {Euphrates} River.”
{After} the king {read this letter, he} sent this reply to them:
My officials carefully read out loud to me the letter that you sent to us.
Then I ordered my officials to search {the records}. I have found out that {what you said is true.} The people of Jerusalem have repeatedly revolted against their rulers, beginning a long time ago.
{In the past,} powerful kings ruled in Jerusalem. They also ruled over the whole province west of the {Euphrates} River. They forced the people there to pay them all kinds of taxes.
Therefore, you must command those Jews to stop rebuilding the city. They will only be allowed to resume if I tell them that they may rebuild it.
Do this immediately, because I do not want those people to do anything more that will cause me to lose {any territory or income}.”

Then King Artaxerxes sent {messengers with} a copy of the letter to Rehum and Shimshai the provincial secretary and their colleagues. As soon as the messengers finished reading it out loud to them, Rehum and Shimshai and their colleagues went quickly to the Jews in Jerusalem, and they forced the Jews to stop rebuilding {the city}.

{Because the enemies of the Jews kept opposing them so strongly in these ways,} the Jews had stopped rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. They did not do any more work to rebuild the temple until the second year after Darius had become the king of Persia.

At that time two prophets were giving messages from God to the Jews living in Jerusalem and in other cities in Judah{, saying that they should continue rebuilding the temple}. Those prophets were Haggai and Zechariah, the son of Iddo. They spoke their messages representing the God whom the people of Israel worshiped, the one who ruled them.

So Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jozadak led many other people to start rebuilding the temple of God in Jerusalem again. God’s prophets Haggai and Zechariah were with them and helping them.

But then Tattenai, the governor of the province west of the Euphrates River, and Shethar-Bozenai went to Jerusalem together with some of their officials and said to the people, “Who has permitted you to do all this work to rebuild this temple?”
They also asked the Jews to tell them the names of the men who were working on this temple.

However, God was taking care of the Jewish leaders, and their enemies did not make them stop {building the temple}. Instead, the enemies sent King Darius a report and waited for him to send back a decree about it. {The decree would either allow the Jewish leaders to finish their work on the temple, or else it would command them to stop their work completely}.

This is a copy of the report that Tattenai, governor of the province of Beyond-the-River, Shethar-Bozenai, and their associates, {who were} the officials of the province of Beyond-the-River, sent to King Darius.
When they sent the report to him, this is what they wrote in it:

We want you to know that we went to the temple of the great God in the province of Judah. The people are building it with huge stones, and they are putting wooden beams in the walls. They are doing this work very carefully, and they are making good progress.
So we asked the Jewish leaders, ‘Who has permitted you to rebuild this temple?’
We also asked them for the names of their leaders so that we could write them down and so that we could inform you who their leaders were.
This is what they told us in reply. They said, ‘We serve the God who created heaven and earth. We are rebuilding his temple, which a great king of Israel originally completed many years ago.

But our ancestors did things that caused God, who is in heaven, to become very angry. So God allowed {the armies of} Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, a Chaldean, to conquer them. His armies destroyed that temple, and they took many of the Israelite people to Babylon.
However, during the first year that Cyrus ruled as king of Babylon, he decreed that our people could rebuild the temple for God.

There had been a lot of containers made of gold and silver in the temple of God. Nebuchadnezzar took them from the temple in Jerusalem and brought them to a temple {for his god} in Babylon. Later, King Cyrus removed those containers from that temple in Babylon and gave them to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed as governor {of Judah}.
King Cyrus told Sheshbazzar to take these containers and put them back in the temple in Jerusalem. He also decreed that the Jews should rebuild the temple at the place where it had been before.

So Sheshbazzar came here to Jerusalem and {supervised the men who} laid the foundation of this temple. And since that time, the people have been working on the temple, but they have not finished it yet.’

Therefore, your Majesty, please order your officials to search in the place in Babylon where you keep the royal records. Have them find out whether or not it is true that King Cyrus decreed that the Jews should rebuild this temple of God in Jerusalem. Then please tell us what you would like us to do about this matter.”
So King Darius commanded his servants to search in the places where he kept important records there in the kingdom of Babylon.
They {searched, and they} found a scroll {that contained the information that they wanted to know} in the fortress city of Ecbatana in the province of Media. This is what that scroll said:

“During the first year that King Cyrus ruled the empire, he sent out a decree concerning the temple of God that was in Jerusalem. He said, ‘I command that the Jews shall build a new temple in the same place where they had previously offered sacrifices. They must make the temple 27 meters high and 27 meters wide.

They must build the temple from large stones. {After putting down} three layers of stones, {the workers must put} a layer of new timber {on top of them}. I will pay for this work with money from the royal treasury.

I also give back {to the Jews} the gold and silver containers that had belonged to the temple of God but that Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon. The Jews must take these and return them to the temple in Jerusalem. The Jews must put each one back in its original place in the temple of God.’”

{After learning this from the scroll, King Darius had a scribe write that information in a letter that he sent to the leaders of the enemies of the Jews in Jerusalem. He also included this message:} “This is a message for you, Tattenai, the governor of {the province} west of the {Euphrates} River, for you, Shethar-Bozenai, and for all of your associates, who are the officials of that province: Stay away from there!

Allow them to continue the work of rebuilding that temple of God. Allow the governor of the Jews and their elders to lead their people in building this new temple on the same site as the former temple.

Furthermore, I command you to help these leaders of the Jews {in the following ways} as they rebuild this temple of God. You must be sure to give these men funds so that they can continue the building work. Take the money from my treasury, from the tribute you collect in {the province} west of the {Euphrates} River.

The priests in Jerusalem need animals to sacrifice as burnt offerings to the God who is in heaven. This may include young bulls or rams or lambs. They may also need wheat, salt, wine, and olive oil {to go with those sacrifices}. Make sure that you diligently give them whatever they demand of those things every day.
When you do that, they will be able to offer sacrifices that please the God who is in heaven, and they will be able to pray that God will bless me and my sons.

This is what I command about anyone who disobeys this decree. My soldiers will pull a beam from his house {and sharpen one end of it}. Then they will bury the other end of the beam in the ground so that it stands upright. Then they will pick that person up and ram his body onto the {sharpened} beam. Then they will completely destroy that person’s house until only a pile of rubble is left, because he disobeyed me.

God himself has chosen that city of Jerusalem as the place where people will honor him. May he get rid of any king or any nation that tries to change this decree or destroy that temple in Jerusalem! I, Darius, make this decree. You must completely obey it.”

Tattenai, the governor of the province west of the Euphrates River, and Shethar-Bozenai and their associates {read the message from King Darius and} immediately obeyed what the message from King Darius commanded them to do.

So the Jewish leaders continued to progress in their work of rebuilding {the temple}. The messages that the prophets Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo preached encouraged them greatly. The people worked until they completed {the temple}, just as their God had commanded them to do, and just as the Persian kings Cyrus and Darius had decreed, and as the Persian king Artaxerxes {would decree later}.
The people finished building this temple on the third day of the month of Adar, during the sixth year that King Darius ruled {the kingdom of Persia}.
Then the people of Israel, {that is,} the priests, the Levites, and everyone else who had returned from Babylonia, joyfully dedicated this temple to God.

During the ceremony to dedicate this temple to God, they sacrificed 100 young bulls, 200 rams, and 400 lambs. They also sacrificed 12 male goats as an offering so that God would forgive the sins of all the people, because that was how many tribes there were in Israel.

Then the Jewish leaders divided the priests and Levites into groups that would take turns serving in the temple of God in Jerusalem. They did this according to what Moses had written {many years previously} in the law.

{To qualify themselves for offering the sacrifices,} all the priests and Levites had already purified themselves by performing the proper rituals. Then they slaughtered the lambs for the benefit of everyone who had returned from Babylonia, for the other priests, and for themselves.

All of the Israelite people celebrated the Passover. This included the Israelites who had returned from Babylonia and the people who had separated themselves from the people of the area around them who worshiped other gods. They separated themselves from those people and joined the Israelites so that they could worship Yahweh, the God whom the Israelite people worshiped.

Then for the next seven days, they joyfully celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread. They were joyful because Yahweh had caused the king of Assyria to be favorable to them. As a result, the king had helped them to rebuild the temple of God, the God whom Israel worshiped.
Many years later, during the time when Artaxerxes was the king of Persia, {there was a man named} Ezra{. He} was a descendant of Seraiah, who was the son of Azariah, who was the son of Hilkiah.
Hilkiah was the son of Shallum, who was the son of Zadok, who was a descendant of Ahitub,
who was a descendant of Amariah, who was the son of Azariah, who was a descendant of Meraioth,
who was the son of Zerahiah, who was the son of Uzzi, who was the son of Bukki,

Ezra {and the group with him} arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the seventh year that Artaxerxes was king.

Consider this: They started out from Babylon on the first day of the first month. They arrived safely in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month of that year. God certainly acted very kindly toward them.

{God made Ezra’s journey successful} because Ezra had devoted himself to studying the laws of Yahweh and understanding how to obey them. He had also devoted himself to teach everything in those laws to the Israelite people.
King Artaxerxes gave a letter to Ezra the priest and scribe who studied what Yahweh had commanded in the law that Yahweh had given to Israel. This is what the letter said:

“This letter is from Artaxerxes, the greatest of the kings. I am giving it to Ezra the priest, who has carefully studied the law that the God who is in heaven gave {to the Israelite people}. Greetings. This is what I want you to know:
